journeyIntro: For navigating parents, siblings and relatives. Build warmth, clarity and healthier family conversations.

lessons.title: Speak Without Blame
lessons.summary: Make requests without starting a family row.

steps.title: Old roles, quick triggers
steps.body: With family we slip into roles we’ve played for years, and small annoyances can spark big rows. A calm, specific request breaks the old script.

steps.prompt: Your younger brother keeps taking your phone charger without asking, and it’s gone again. What do you say?

options.text: “You’re so selfish, you always do this.”
options.why: Calling him selfish makes it about his character, so he’ll defend himself, not change.

options.text: Hide the charger and say nothing.
options.why: It solves tonight, but he never learns it bothers you, and the habit carries on.

options.text: “Can you ask before borrowing my charger? I keep running out of battery.”
options.why: It’s specific about the action and why it matters, without labelling him as a person.

steps.prompt: Describe the action, not the person.
steps.why: A clear action is easy to do; a label just starts an argument about who they are.

steps.prompt: Which family member is hardest for you to ask things of?
steps.reply: That’s often where the oldest patterns live. Short, specific requests help most there.

steps.prompt: Blame, or an “I” statement?

cards.text: “I get stressed when my charger goes missing.”
“I’d like you to ask before borrowing things.”

steps.why: “I” statements share how it affects you and what you’d like, so family can listen instead of defending themselves.

steps.body: Make one specific, calm request to a family member today, describing the action rather than their character.

lessons.title: Sibling Squabbles
lessons.summary: Grown-up siblings can still fall into old roles.

steps.title: Old roles die hard
steps.body: Around siblings, adults can slip back into being “the bossy one” or “the baby”. Noticing the old role, and choosing to speak as the adult you are now, changes how they respond.

steps.prompt: Your older sister corrects how you’re cooking at a family dinner, like she did when you were kids. What’s best?

options.text: “I’ve got this, thanks. Want to help set the table?”
options.why: Calm and adult, and it gives her a role without a fight.

options.text: “You always treat me like I’m ten!”
options.why: True or not, it pulls you both straight back into the old dynamic.

options.text: Hand her the spoon and sulk.
options.why: Giving in while seething keeps the old pattern going.

steps.prompt: Speak as your adult self.
steps.before: I know you mean well, but I’d like to do it my
steps.why: A calm, adult tone helps everyone step out of childhood roles.

steps.prompt: What role did you play growing up?
steps.reply: Knowing your old role helps you notice when you slip back into it.

steps.prompt: Adult response, or old childhood role?

cards.text: “I see it differently. Can we talk?”
Bringing up who got more toys

steps.why: Responding as the adult you are now breaks old patterns and builds a better sibling relationship.

steps.body: Next time a sibling pushes an old button, pause and respond as the adult you are today.

lessons.title: Family Group Chats
lessons.summary: Keep the family chat warm, not tense.

steps.title: Group chats need care
steps.body: Family group chats are great for photos and plans, but tone is easy to misread and everyone sees every reply. Big feelings are usually better one-to-one.

steps.prompt: In the family chat, your brother posts that you never help with Mum’s shopping. You’re upset. What’s best?

options.text: Reply in the chat listing everything you do.
options.why: A public defence can turn into a family-wide argument.

options.text: Leave the chat.
options.why: It avoids the moment but leaves everyone confused.

options.text: Message him privately: “That stung. Can we talk about sharing Mum’s shopping?”
options.why: Taking it private lets you sort it out without an audience.

steps.prompt: Take it private.
steps.why: Private chats lower defences and keep the family chat friendly.

steps.prompt: What’s your family chat mostly used for?
steps.reply: Keeping it light and taking tough topics elsewhere helps it stay a happy place.

steps.prompt: Match each moment with a better place for it.
steps.why: Choosing the right place for each kind of message prevents misunderstandings and public arguments.

steps.body: If something in the family chat upsets you, reply privately rather than in the group.

lessons.title: Listen Across Generations
lessons.summary: Understand a relative before responding.

steps.title: Worry often sounds like criticism
steps.body: When a parent questions your choices, it can feel like judgement. Often underneath is worry, shaped by the world they grew up in.

steps.prompt: Your mum keeps questioning your decision to leave a stable job for a start-up. What’s the most helpful response?

options.text: “It sounds like you’re worried. What worries you most?”
options.why: Naming the worry and asking about it helps her feel heard, so she can soften too.

options.text: “You just don’t get how work is now.”
options.why: It may feel true, but it shuts her out and turns her worry into an argument.

options.text: Agree you’ll rethink it, just to end the conversation.
options.why: It buys quiet now, but the worry stays unspoken and the topic will come back.

steps.title: Understanding isn’t giving in
steps.body: You can hear their concern fully and still make your own choice. “I see why that worries you. I’ve thought it through, and here’s why.”

steps.prompt: Show you understand.
steps.before: I can see why you’d be
steps.why: Naming their worry makes them feel understood, even if you still disagree.

steps.prompt: When a relative questions your choices, how do you usually react?
steps.reply: Very common. Asking what’s behind their concern can turn a lecture into a real conversation.

steps.title: A call with Gran

lines.text: Your cousin says you’re seeing a therapist now?
In my day we just got on with things.

steps.prompt: What do you say?

options.text: Times have changed, Gran. It’s normal now.
options.why: It’s true, but it shuts her view down rather than understanding it.

options.text: Please don’t start, Gran.
options.why: Ending the talk leaves her worry unspoken and the gap between you wider.

options.text: You did have to get on with a lot. What was that like for you?
options.reaction: Oh, it was hard, love. Nobody talked about feelings back then…
options.why: Curiosity about her experience builds a bridge, and she may hear your side better after.

steps.body: Next time a relative questions a choice of yours, ask what’s behind their concern before explaining yourself.

lessons.title: Ask About Their Stories
lessons.summary: Older relatives hold stories worth hearing.

steps.title: Stories connect generations
steps.body: Grandparents and parents often have stories nobody has asked about: their first job, how they met, hard times they got through. Asking shows respect and brings you closer.

steps.prompt: You’re visiting your grandad, who often sits quietly. What’s a great way to connect?

options.text: Watch TV together in silence.
options.why: Comfortable, but you miss the chance to really connect.

options.text: “What was your first job like, Grandad?”
options.why: An open question about his life invites stories he may love to share.

options.text: Tell him all about your week.
options.why: Nice to share, but asking about him shows you’re interested in his life too.

steps.prompt: Invite a story.
steps.before: What was it like when you were
steps.why: Questions about their past often open up memories they rarely get to share.

steps.prompt: Which relative’s stories would you love to hear?
steps.reply: Ask them one question next time you see them. You might be surprised.

steps.prompt: Opens up a story, or closes it down?

cards.text: Checking your phone as they talk

steps.why: Curious questions and full attention make older relatives feel valued, and keep family stories alive.

steps.body: Ask an older relative one question about their past this week, and listen to the whole answer.

lessons.title: When Parents Give Advice
lessons.summary: Hear the care behind it, even if you disagree.

steps.title: Advice is often love in disguise
steps.body: Parents’ advice can feel like criticism, but it often comes from worry or care. Hearing the care first makes it easier to respond calmly, even if you choose differently.

steps.prompt: Your dad keeps telling you to buy a house instead of renting. You’re happy renting. What’s best?

options.text: “Dad, I know you want me to be secure. I’ve thought about it, and renting suits me now.”
options.why: You name the care behind his advice and calmly explain your choice.

options.text: “Can you just stop?”
options.why: It ends the conversation but may leave him hurt or worried.

options.text: Agree, then do nothing.
options.why: Saying yes when you mean no often leads to the same advice again.

steps.prompt: Name the care first.
steps.before: I know you’re saying this because you
steps.why: Acknowledging their care helps them hear your view without feeling dismissed.

steps.prompt: Which topic do you get the most advice about?
steps.reply: Preparing a calm, kind answer for that topic makes it much easier next time.

steps.title: Mum’s advice

lines.text: Are you still working those late shifts? You’ll wear yourself out.
You should really look for something else 😟

steps.prompt: You like your job. Reply:

options.text: Mum, stop worrying about me!
options.reaction: I can’t help it, I’m your mum.
options.why: It brushes off her care rather than easing it.

options.text: I know you worry, that’s lovely. I’m enjoying it and looking after myself. Call Sunday?
options.why: You thank her care, reassure her and stay true to your choice.

options.text: Fine, I’ll look.
options.reaction: Good! I’ll send you some ads.
options.why: Agreeing to keep the peace often brings more of the same advice.

steps.body: Next time a parent gives advice, thank them for caring before you share your view.

lessons.title: Show Up in Small Ways
lessons.summary: Little moments can soften distance.

steps.title: Little and often
steps.body: Family closeness rarely comes from big reunions alone. A five-minute call or a funny photo sent their way keeps the thread between you warm.

steps.prompt: Your grandad calls while you’re in the middle of cooking. What’s the kindest response?

options.text: Answer and half-listen while you chop.
options.why: He may well hear the distraction, and the call can leave you both feeling unsatisfied.

options.text: “Lovely to hear you! I’m cooking, can I ring you back at seven?”
options.why: It’s warm, honest and gives a time, so he gets your full attention instead of half of it.

options.text: Let it ring and plan to call at the weekend.
options.why: Weekends have a way of slipping, and he may worry or feel forgotten in the meantime.

steps.prompt: Offer your full attention later.
steps.why: A set time shows they matter and makes it far more likely the call actually happens.

steps.prompt: Which small gesture would mean most to someone in your family?
steps.reply: Lovely. Small, regular gestures like that keep family bonds warm between big moments.

steps.prompt: Match each relative with a small way to show up.
steps.why: Showing up doesn’t need grand gestures; small, well-matched moments add up to feeling cared for.

steps.body: Send a relative a short message or call today, just to say you were thinking of them.

lessons.title: Family Rituals
lessons.summary: Small traditions hold families together.

steps.title: Rituals create belonging
steps.body: Sunday calls, pancake Saturdays, a yearly walk on Grandma’s birthday. Simple family rituals give everyone something to look forward to and a sense of belonging.

steps.prompt: Your family only gets together at Christmas, and you’d like to see each other more. What’s most likely to work?

options.text: Plan a big summer reunion with everyone.
options.why: Lovely, but big events are hard to organise and easy to cancel.

options.text: A monthly video call on the first Sunday.
options.why: Simple and regular, so it’s easy to keep going.

options.text: Wait for someone else to organise something.
options.why: If everyone waits, nothing happens.

steps.prompt: Make it regular.
steps.why: Regular rituals become part of family life, rather than one-off events.

steps.prompt: Which family ritual do you love, or wish you had?
steps.reply: Suggesting a small version this month could be the start of something special.

steps.prompt: Match each family with a ritual that could fit.
steps.why: The best rituals fit how your family actually lives, so they’re easy to keep.

steps.body: Suggest one small, regular ritual to your family this week.

lessons.title: Long-Distance Family
lessons.summary: Stay close when you live far apart.

steps.title: Distance needs a little planning
steps.body: When family lives far away, it’s easy to drift into only talking at birthdays. Small, regular touches, a voice note, a photo, a quick call, keep you part of each other’s lives.

steps.prompt: Your parents moved to another country. You feel guilty you rarely call. What helps most?

options.text: Wait until you have time for a long call.
options.why: Long calls are hard to schedule, so they keep getting pushed back.

options.text: Send short voice notes or photos a few times a week.
options.why: Small, regular contact keeps you close without needing big chunks of time.

options.text: Feel bad, but do nothing.
options.why: Guilt alone doesn’t bring you closer. A small step does.

steps.prompt: A quick touch.
steps.why: Small everyday moments help faraway family feel included.

steps.prompt: How do you stay in touch with faraway family?
steps.reply: Picking one easy habit and doing it weekly makes a real difference.

steps.prompt: Keeps you close, or lets you drift?

cards.text: Watching the same show and chatting about it

steps.why: Little, regular moments of contact matter more than rare long calls.

steps.body: Send a faraway relative a quick photo or voice note today.

lessons.title: You Can Say No
lessons.summary: Care does not mean unlimited availability.

steps.title: Love and limits can coexist
steps.body: Family expectations can feel like duties you can’t refuse. But you can care deeply and still decide how much time and energy you can give.

steps.prompt: Your aunt expects you at every Sunday lunch, and you’re worn out. What’s the healthiest way to respond?

options.text: Keep going every week and quietly resent it.
options.why: Resentment tends to leak out in other ways, and you’ll enjoy the lunches less.

options.text: “I’ll come this Sunday, but I can’t manage every week.”
options.why: It’s warm and clear: you show you care while being honest about what you can give.

options.text: Invent an illness each time to avoid saying no.
options.why: Excuses pile up and are stressful to keep up; an honest limit is easier in the long run.

steps.title: Short and kind is enough
steps.body: You don’t need a long defence. One clear sentence, said kindly, then let it be. Over-explaining invites debate about whether your reasons are good enough.

steps.title: When family feels unsafe
steps.body: Healthy families never involve fear, control or harm. If someone in yours makes you feel unsafe, talk to someone you trust or a local support line.

steps.prompt: Keep the limit short.
steps.before: I can’t make it this week,
words: but I’d love to next month
steps.answer: but I’d love to next month
steps.why: It’s clear and warm, and offers what you can do rather than only what you can’t.

steps.prompt: Saying no to a family plan. Put these in order.
steps.why: Warmth first, then a clear no, keeps it kind; offering an alternative shows you still care about them.

steps.body: State one family limit this week in a single kind sentence, without a long explanation.

lessons.title: Unwanted Advice
lessons.summary: Set a kind limit on comments you didn’t ask for.

steps.title: You can close a topic kindly
steps.body: Relatives sometimes comment on your weight, relationships or parenting. You can set a limit warmly, without a fight: thank them, close the topic, and move on.

steps.prompt: At every visit, your aunt asks when you’re having a baby. It hurts. What’s a kind, firm response?

options.text: Laugh it off every time.
options.why: It keeps the peace but the comments, and the hurt, keep coming.

options.text: “That’s private for us. Anyway, how’s your garden doing?”
options.why: Warm, clear and it moves the conversation on without drama.

options.text: Snap: “Mind your own business!”
options.why: Understandable, but it may cause a bigger family rift.

steps.prompt: Close the topic warmly.
steps.before: I’d rather not talk about that, but thanks for
steps.why: Thanking them softens the limit, so it’s easier to hear.

steps.prompt: Which comment do you hear most from family?
steps.reply: Having one calm, ready-made reply makes it much easier to handle next time.

steps.prompt: Handling an unwanted comment. Put these in order.
items: Say it’s not up for discussion
Repeat calmly if it comes up again
steps.why: A calm pause, a clear line and a new topic set the limit kindly. Repeating it gently helps it stick.

steps.body: Prepare one kind, firm sentence for the family comment that bothers you most.

lessons.title: Holidays Without Burnout
lessons.summary: Plan family holidays that leave room to breathe.

steps.title: Holidays can be a lot
steps.body: Big family holidays mean travel, cooking and lots of people. Planning breaks, sharing jobs and knowing your limits helps you enjoy it instead of just getting through it.

steps.prompt: You’re hosting Christmas again and already feel exhausted. What’s healthiest?

options.text: Do it all yourself. It’s easier.
options.why: Doing everything alone often ends in burnout and resentment.

options.text: Cancel Christmas this year.
options.why: Drastic. There’s usually a middle ground.

options.text: Ask everyone to bring a dish and help clear up.
options.why: Sharing the load lets you enjoy the day too.

steps.prompt: Share the work.
steps.why: A specific ask makes it easy for family to help.

steps.prompt: What drains you most at family holidays?
steps.reply: Planning around that one thing can make the whole holiday feel lighter.

steps.prompt: Helps you cope, or leads to burnout?

cards.text: Planning a quiet walk each day

steps.why: Breaks, shared jobs and clear plans let you enjoy family holidays instead of being worn out by them.

steps.body: Before your next family gathering, plan one break for yourself and ask for help with one job.

lessons.title: Money and Family
lessons.summary: Be generous within limits you can keep.

steps.title: Money can strain family ties
steps.body: Lending to family can be kind, but unclear terms often cause resentment. Decide what you can afford, be clear about whether it’s a gift or a loan, and protect the relationship.

steps.prompt: Your cousin asks to borrow a large amount for a car. You could afford a smaller sum. What’s best?

options.text: Lend it all and hope they pay you back.
options.why: If repayment is slow, it can sour things between you.

options.text: “I can’t lend that much, but I could give you a smaller amount as a gift.”
options.why: Generous within your limits, and a gift means no awkward debt between you.

options.text: Say you have no money at all.
options.why: Untrue, and it could come out later.

steps.prompt: Be clear about it.
steps.before: Is this a gift or a
steps.why: Agreeing upfront avoids misunderstandings that can damage family ties.

steps.prompt: How do you feel about lending money to family?
steps.reply: Deciding your own rule in advance makes these moments much easier.

steps.prompt: Match each situation with a healthy approach.
steps.why: Clear, kind limits let you support family without money damaging the relationship.

steps.body: Decide your personal rule for lending to family, so you’re ready next time someone asks.

lessons.title: Rebuild Reliability
lessons.summary: Let trust return through consistent actions.

steps.title: Family remembers
steps.body: In families, one missed promise can echo older ones. That makes small, steady follow-through especially powerful for rebuilding trust.

steps.prompt: You promised to pick up your dad’s prescription and forgot. He’s now out of tablets. What helps most?

options.text: “My sister was supposed to remind me.”
options.why: Shifting the blame dodges the moment and can stir up old sibling tensions too.

options.text: “I’m sorry, I forgot. I’ll collect it first thing tomorrow.”
options.why: It owns the slip and offers a concrete fix, which is how reliability gets rebuilt.

options.text: “Come on, it’s only family, it’s fine.”
options.why: Family promises matter just as much; brushing it off tells him he’s not a priority.

steps.prompt: Offer a realistic fix.
words: try to get round to it
steps.why: A specific, doable plan shows you mean it; vague promises sound like the same slip again.

steps.prompt: Which family promise do you most often let slip?
steps.reply: Pick that one and make it small and specific. Steady follow-through rebuilds trust quickly.

steps.prompt: Builds reliability or wears it down?

cards.text: Setting a reminder the moment you agree
Saying yes to everything, then forgetting
Telling them early if you can’t make it

steps.why: Being reliable is less about never slipping and more about honest yeses, reminders and owning it when you do.

steps.body: Choose one small family commitment this week and follow through exactly as you said.

lessons.title: Caring for Ageing Parents
lessons.summary: Be someone they can count on, without losing yourself.

steps.title: Steady support matters most
steps.body: As parents get older, small, reliable help, a weekly call, help with appointments, often means more than big gestures. Being steady also means being honest about what you can manage.

steps.prompt: Your mum needs more help since her fall, and you’re already stretched. What’s best?

options.text: Promise to visit every day, even if you can’t.
options.why: Promises you can’t keep lead to letdowns and guilt.

options.text: Commit to two set visits a week, and ask siblings to share the rest.
options.why: Reliable and realistic, and it shares the care fairly.

options.text: Leave it to whoever lives closest.
options.why: It can leave one person carrying everything.

steps.prompt: Promise what you can keep.
steps.why: Specific, realistic promises are the ones you can reliably keep.

steps.prompt: What’s one small, steady way you could support an older relative?
steps.placeholder: e.g. a call every Sunday evening

steps.prompt: Sharing care for a parent. Put these in order.
steps.why: Starting with their needs and your real limits leads to care that lasts, without burnout.

steps.body: Offer one specific, regular bit of help to an older relative this week.

lessons.title: Keep Family Confidences
lessons.summary: What’s shared in trust stays in trust.

steps.title: Families talk
steps.body: News travels fast in families. If a relative tells you something privately and it spreads, they’ll stop confiding in you. Keeping confidences makes you the person they can rely on.

steps.prompt: Your brother tells you he’s struggling with debt. Your mum asks why he seems stressed. What do you say?

options.text: Tell her. She’s his mum and should know.
options.why: Well-meant, but it breaks his trust in you.

options.text: “Maybe ask him gently? I think he’d appreciate it coming from you.”
options.why: You keep his confidence and encourage her to reach out herself.

options.text: “Nothing’s wrong, he’s fine.”
options.why: Lying can backfire when the truth comes out.

steps.prompt: Check before sharing.
steps.before: Are you okay with me telling
steps.why: Asking first respects their choice about who knows.

steps.prompt: Who in your family confides in you most?
steps.reply: Keeping their trust is one of the quietest, strongest ways to stay close.

steps.prompt: Keeping a confidence, or breaking it?

cards.text: Sharing it “so we can all help”

steps.why: Even well-meant sharing breaks trust. Keeping confidences makes you someone family can turn to.

steps.body: If a relative has told you something private, quietly decide it stays with you.

lessons.title: Disagree Without Winning
lessons.summary: Keep respect when family views differ.

steps.title: Not every debate needs a winner
steps.body: Family meals can turn into battlegrounds over politics or life choices. Often the goal isn’t to change minds, but to keep respect intact.

steps.prompt: At a family dinner, your uncle starts criticising your choices in front of everyone. What’s the best move?

options.text: “We see this differently, and I’d rather not debate it tonight.”
options.why: It’s calm and firm: you name the difference and step out without escalating.

options.text: Argue it out loudly until he backs down.
options.why: Winning at the table rarely changes minds and usually ruins the meal for everyone.

options.text: Fire back with a dig about his own life.
options.why: It may feel satisfying, but it escalates fast and becomes the story of the evening.

steps.title: Have an exit line ready
steps.body: A go-to phrase helps when you’re put on the spot: “Let’s agree to differ,” or “Can we talk about something else?” Then change the subject.

steps.prompt: Step out of the debate.
steps.why: It acknowledges the difference without either of you having to lose face.

steps.prompt: Which topics most often spark family arguments for you?
steps.reply: Knowing your hot topics lets you plan your exit line before you even sit down.

steps.title: The family group chat

lines.text: Read this article. It’ll set you straight 😉
Can’t believe you young people think otherwise.

steps.prompt: You see it very differently. Reply:

options.text: This article is nonsense and you know it.
options.why: Attacking it turns the chat into a contest that nobody wins.

options.text: I see it differently, Dad, but I’d like to hear why it matters to you. Call later?
options.reaction: Alright, I’ll ring you after dinner.
options.why: You stay honest and curious, and move it out of the group chat to a real talk.

options.text: *leaves the group chat*
options.why: Walking out avoids the moment but leaves everyone confused and tense.

steps.body: Choose one calm exit line for heated family topics, and use it the next time a debate starts to boil.

lessons.title: Values That Differ
lessons.summary: Love family members whose choices aren’t yours.

steps.title: Different, not wrong
steps.body: Family members may choose different faiths, careers or ways of living. You don’t have to agree to stay close. Respecting their right to choose keeps the door open.

steps.prompt: Your parents are upset you’ve chosen not to marry your long-term partner. What’s the best response?

options.text: “I know it matters to you. It’s our choice, and we’re really happy.”
options.why: You respect their feelings while standing calmly by your choice.

options.text: “Your views are so old-fashioned.”
options.why: Mocking their values pushes them away rather than helping them understand.

options.text: Avoid seeing them until they accept it.
options.why: Distance may cool things, but it also keeps you apart.

steps.prompt: Respect both sides.
steps.why: Naming the difference with love keeps the relationship stronger than the disagreement.

steps.prompt: Where do you and your family differ most?
steps.reply: Remembering what you share, beyond that one area, helps keep things warm.

steps.prompt: Match each clash with a respectful response.

pairs.b: “I respect what it means to you.”

steps.why: Respectful words let family members disagree on big things and still feel loved.

steps.body: Tell a relative you disagree with that you respect their right to choose, and mean it.

lessons.title: Cool Down at Gatherings
lessons.summary: Step away before a family dinner boils over.

steps.title: Gatherings can heat up fast
steps.body: Tiredness, old tensions and a few drinks can turn a family meal tense. Noticing the heat rising and stepping away for a few minutes can save the whole day.

steps.prompt: At Sunday lunch, your uncle starts a heated debate and you feel your temper rising. What do you do?

options.text: Argue back until he gives in.
options.why: In front of everyone, it’s likely to escalate rather than end.

options.text: “I’m going to grab some air.” Then step outside for a few minutes.
options.why: A short break calms you down without making a scene.

options.text: Sit in silence and fume.
options.why: Bottling it up can leak out later in a bigger way.

steps.prompt: A calm exit line.
steps.before: I’m just going to get some
steps.why: A neutral reason lets you step away without adding fuel.

steps.prompt: What usually sparks tension at your family gatherings?
steps.reply: Planning your calm exit for that moment makes gatherings much easier.

steps.title: Heated dinner

lines.text: Young people today don’t know what hard work is.
Back in my day we didn’t complain.

steps.prompt: You feel annoyed. Reply:

options.text: That’s rubbish, Rob, and you know it.
options.why: It turns a passing comment into a full-blown argument.

options.text: Mm. Anyone want more potatoes?
options.why: A light change of subject cools things without a fight.

options.text: (You storm off.)
options.why: Leaving abruptly can create more tension than the comment did.

steps.body: Before your next family gathering, plan one way to step away if things get tense.

lessons.title: Repair a Family Hurt
lessons.summary: Take responsibility for your part.

steps.title: Small digs leave marks
steps.body: A throwaway comment between siblings can sting for years. Naming your part, even long after, can soften things more than you expect.

steps.prompt: You made a dismissive comment about your sister’s new business, and she went quiet. What repairs it?

options.text: “Sorry you took it that way.”
options.why: It sounds like an apology but puts the problem on her reaction, not your words.

options.text: Avoid her until it blows over.
options.why: Family hurts rarely just blow over; they tend to resurface in the next argument.

options.text: “That comment was unfair. I’m sorry I dismissed something you care about.”
options.why: It names the specific hurt and its impact, without excuses, which makes it believable.

steps.title: Then show interest
steps.body: After apologising, show the respect the comment lacked: ask about the business, celebrate a win. Actions help the words stick.

steps.prompt: Is there a family hurt you’d like to repair? What would you say?
Match each defensive line with a repair.
steps.why: Repairs take the hurt seriously instead of brushing it off, which is what lets family trust you again.

steps.body: If it feels right, apologise to one family member for something specific, without adding “but”.

lessons.title: Old Childhood Hurts
lessons.summary: Some old wounds deserve a gentle conversation.

steps.title: Old hurts can still sting
steps.body: Something a parent said or did years ago can still hurt. Raising it gently, focusing on how it felt rather than blame, can bring understanding, though it may take more than one talk.

steps.prompt: You still feel hurt that your parents missed your school play for work. You’d like to talk about it. What’s best?

options.text: Bring it up in an argument about something else.
options.why: It’ll feel like an attack, and the real hurt may get lost.

options.text: “Can I share something from when I was little? It still means a lot to me.”
options.why: A gentle opening invites them to listen rather than defend.

options.text: Keep it to yourself. It’s in the past.
options.why: Sometimes fine, but if it still hurts, it may be worth sharing.

steps.prompt: Focus on feelings.
steps.before: When you missed my play, I felt
steps.why: Sharing how it felt, rather than what they did wrong, makes it easier to hear.

steps.prompt: Is there an old family hurt you’d like to talk about? What would you want them to know?
steps.placeholder: e.g. how much it meant when…

steps.prompt: Talking about an old hurt. Put these in order.
steps.why: Calm timing and feelings-first sharing make understanding possible, even about something from long ago.

steps.body: If an old hurt still weighs on you, write down what you’d want to say before deciding whether to share it.

lessons.title: Reconnect After Distance
lessons.summary: Reach out after a long family silence.

steps.title: Someone has to go first
steps.body: After a falling-out or years of drifting, getting back in touch can feel daunting. A short, warm message with no blame often opens the door more than a long explanation.

steps.prompt: You haven’t spoken to your cousin in three years since a family argument. You miss her. What do you send?

options.text: A long message explaining who was right.
options.why: Reopening the argument can close the door again.

options.text: Nothing. She should reach out first.
options.why: If you both wait, the silence continues.

options.text: “I’ve been thinking of you and I miss you. Would you like to catch up?”
options.why: Warm, simple and blame-free, which makes it easy to say yes.

steps.prompt: Lead with warmth.
steps.why: Saying you miss them focuses on the relationship, not the old disagreement.

steps.prompt: Is there a relative you’ve drifted from?
steps.reply: A short, warm message is often all it takes to start again.

steps.title: First message in years

lines.text: Hi Sam, I’ve been thinking of you. I miss you. Would you like to catch up?
Wow, hi. I’ve missed you too. I’m sorry about how things went.

steps.prompt: Reply:

options.text: Me too. I’d love to put it behind us. Coffee next week?
options.why: You meet her apology with warmth and move towards reconnecting.

options.text: Well, you did say some hurtful things.
options.why: Going back over old wounds can stall a fresh start.

options.text: Okay.
options.why: A flat reply can make her unsure you really want to reconnect.

steps.body: If there’s a relative you miss, send them a short, warm message this week.

lessons.title: Respect Different Roles
lessons.summary: You can help without fixing everyone.

steps.title: Stuck in the middle
steps.body: Many people end up as the family go-between, passing messages and smoothing things over. It’s exhausting, and it rarely solves the real problem.

steps.prompt: Your mum and your brother aren’t speaking, and each keeps asking you to pass on messages. What helps most?

options.text: Pass on every message to keep the peace.
options.why: Messages change as they travel, and you end up holding everyone’s frustration.

options.text: Pick the side you agree with and back them.
options.why: Taking sides can damage your own relationship with the other person for a long time.

options.text: “I love you both, but I can’t be the messenger. Please talk to each other.”
options.why: It shows care for both while handing the conversation back to the people who need to have it.

steps.prompt: Hand it back kindly.
steps.before: I care about you both, so please
steps.why: It returns the conversation to them, which is where it can actually be resolved.

steps.prompt: What role do you often play in your family?
steps.reply: Roles can be loving and tiring at once. You’re allowed to step out of one now and then.

steps.prompt: Your job, or not your job?

cards.text: Telling each how the rift affects you
Choosing a side to keep the peace

steps.why: You can care about both people and share your feelings without carrying their conflict for them.

steps.body: This week, gently step out of one family conversation that isn’t yours to manage.

lessons.title: Sharing Care Fairly
lessons.summary: Siblings can share family duties without resentment.

steps.title: Fairness needs a conversation
steps.body: Often one sibling ends up doing most of the caring, hosting or organising. Instead of quietly resenting it, an honest talk about sharing the load protects both your energy and your relationships.

steps.prompt: You do almost all the driving for your dad’s appointments, while your sister lives further away. What’s best?

options.text: Keep doing it and quietly resent her.
options.why: Resentment grows and often bursts out later.

options.text: “I’m finding the driving a lot. Could you handle the phone calls and bookings?”
options.why: Honest and practical, and it gives her a fair way to help from afar.

options.text: Tell Dad she doesn’t care.
options.why: It hurts both of them and doesn’t fix the load.

steps.prompt: Ask for a fair share.
steps.why: Naming a specific task makes it easy for them to help, wherever they live.

steps.prompt: How fairly is family care shared in your family?
steps.reply: One honest conversation can make the load feel much lighter.

steps.prompt: Shares the load, or overloads one person?

cards.text: A shared calendar of who does what
“You live closest, so you do it.”

steps.why: Fair sharing looks different for everyone, but it always starts with an honest conversation.

steps.body: If you carry most of a family task, ask a sibling to take on one specific part of it.

lessons.title: Grown-Up Children
lessons.summary: Relate to grown children as the adults they are.

steps.title: From parent to friend
steps.body: When children grow up, the relationship has to change. Offering support instead of instructions, and asking before advising, helps adult children want to stay close.

steps.prompt: Your adult son is moving in with his girlfriend, and you have doubts. What’s best?

options.text: List all your concerns so he knows the risks.
options.why: A list of worries can feel like disapproval of his choice.

options.text: “Congratulations! I’m here if you ever want to talk things through.”
options.why: You respect his choice and leave the door open for support.

options.text: Refuse to help him move.
options.why: Withholding support often pushes adult children away.

steps.prompt: Ask before advising.
steps.why: Asking first treats them as an adult who chooses what help they want.

steps.prompt: In your family, which shift is hardest?
steps.reply: Noticing it is the first step to a more adult-to-adult relationship.

steps.prompt: Match each controlling line with a supportive one.
steps.why: Supportive words show trust, which makes grown children far more likely to share and stay close.

steps.body: Next time a grown family member shares a decision, ask if they want your view before giving it.

lessons.title: Ask, Don’t Assume
lessons.summary: Learn what support a relative wants.

steps.title: Help that fits
steps.body: Family often show love by jumping in to help. But the help someone wants might be a listening ear, not a plan. Asking first makes it land.

steps.prompt: Your grown-up son seems stressed about moving house. What’s the most helpful thing to do?

options.text: Book a removal firm for him as a surprise.
options.why: Kind, but taking over can make an adult child feel you don’t trust them to manage.

options.text: “Would it help more if I listened, or if I helped with the move?”
options.why: It lets him choose the support he needs, so your help is welcome rather than overwhelming.

options.text: Tell him how you handled moving at his age.
options.why: Your experience may help later, but leading with it can feel like a lecture right now.

steps.prompt: Offer a choice.
steps.why: Offering both options shows respect for how they want to handle their own situation.

steps.prompt: When a relative is struggling, what do you tend to offer first?
steps.reply: All useful at the right time. Asking which they need now is the kindest first step.

steps.title: Big news

lines.text: I don’t think I want to go to uni any more.

steps.prompt: What do you reply?

options.text: I’m not mad. Thanks for telling me. What’s making you feel that way?
options.reaction: It’s a lot… can we talk tonight? 💛
options.why: You calm her fear first, then ask instead of assuming, so she feels safe to share.

options.text: Don’t be silly, of course you’re going.
options.why: Deciding for her shuts the conversation down before you know what’s going on.

options.text: Is this because of that new friend of yours?
options.reaction: No! Why do you always do that?
options.why: Guessing the cause feels like blame and makes her less likely to open up.

steps.body: When a relative seems stressed, ask whether they’d like you to listen or help, before doing either.

lessons.title: Check In on Siblings
lessons.summary: Busy lives can hide what siblings are going through.

steps.title: Siblings drift without noticing
steps.body: As adults, siblings get busy with work, partners and kids. A simple “How are you really?” every so often keeps you close, and lets them know you’re there.

steps.prompt: Your brother has gone quiet in the family chat for weeks. What’s best?

options.text: Assume he’s just busy.
options.why: Maybe, but a quiet sibling might also be struggling.

options.text: “Haven’t heard from you in a while. How are you really doing?”
options.why: A gentle, personal check-in shows you care and makes it easy to open up.

options.text: Post in the group chat asking why he’s ignoring everyone.
options.why: Calling him out publicly can make him pull back further.

steps.prompt: Ask for real.
steps.why: Adding “really” shows you want the honest answer, not just “fine”.

steps.prompt: When did you last properly catch up with a sibling?
steps.reply: If it’s been a while, a short, caring message is a great place to start.

steps.prompt: Real check-in, or surface-level?

cards.text: A call just to say hi

steps.why: Real check-ins invite honest answers. Surface contact is nice, but it rarely shows how someone is doing.

steps.body: Send a sibling or close relative a “how are you really?” message today.

lessons.title: Hear Kids Out
lessons.summary: Children open up when they feel heard, not judged.

steps.title: Listen before you lecture
steps.body: When children share a problem, adults often jump to advice or a telling-off. Listening first, and showing you understand, makes children far more likely to keep talking to you.

steps.prompt: Your 12-year-old niece says, “Everyone at school hates me.” What’s the best first response?

options.text: “That’s not true, don’t be silly.”
options.why: It dismisses her feelings, so she may stop sharing.

options.text: “Just ignore them and make new friends.”
options.why: Advice too soon can feel like you’re not really listening.

options.text: “That sounds really lonely. What happened?”
options.why: You name her feeling and invite her to tell you more.

steps.prompt: Name their feeling.
steps.why: Naming the feeling helps children feel understood, and calmer.

steps.prompt: When a child shares a worry, your instinct is to…
steps.reply: Every instinct comes from care. Listening first makes the rest work better.

steps.prompt: Match each worry with a listening response.
steps.why: Listening responses help children feel safe to share, which keeps them coming to you as they grow.

steps.body: Next time a child in your family shares a worry, name their feeling before offering any advice.

lessons.title: Make Room for Change
lessons.summary: Let family bonds grow as people change.

steps.title: Families keep changing shape
steps.body: New partners, children, jobs and cities change how families spend time together. Closeness lasts when we adapt instead of holding on to the old way.

steps.prompt: Since having a baby, your sister rarely makes it to family visits. What’s the most helpful response?

options.text: “We miss you! What would make staying in touch easier right now?”
options.why: It shows she’s missed and invites her to shape a way of connecting that fits her life.

options.text: “You’ve forgotten about the rest of us.”
options.why: Guilt adds pressure at an already demanding time and can push her further away.

options.text: Stop inviting her, since she won’t come anyway.
options.why: She may feel left out, and it’s much harder to find your way back later.

steps.title: New ways to stay close
steps.body: A video call at bath time, visiting her instead, a family group chat. Flexible connection often beats the old traditions when life changes.

steps.prompt: Which family member’s life has changed, and how could you stay close?
A relative’s life has changed. Put these in order.
steps.why: Changing the plan to fit their new life, and keeping the invitation open, keeps you close through the shift.

steps.body: Suggest one new, flexible way to stay connected with a family member whose life has changed.

lessons.title: Welcome New Members
lessons.summary: New partners and in-laws change the family shape.

steps.title: Families grow and shift
steps.body: When someone marries in or a new partner arrives, the family’s rhythm changes. Making them feel welcome, and being patient as everyone adjusts, helps the whole family grow closer.

steps.prompt: Your brother’s new wife seems shy at family events and often sits apart. What’s a kind thing to do?

options.text: Leave her be. She’ll join in when she’s ready.
options.why: Some space is fine, but a warm invitation helps her feel included.

options.text: Sit with her and ask about her family’s traditions.
options.why: A friendly, curious chat helps her feel welcome and valued.

options.text: Ask your brother why she isn’t more sociable.
options.why: It can sound like criticism and put him in an awkward spot.

steps.prompt: Make them welcome.
steps.why: Saying it out loud helps a newcomer feel truly accepted.

steps.prompt: How does your family usually welcome newcomers?
steps.reply: One person’s warmth can set the tone for everyone else.

steps.prompt: Welcoming, or leaves them on the outside?

cards.text: Adding them to the family chat
Talking about exes in front of them

steps.why: Small, thoughtful gestures help new family members feel they belong, which strengthens the whole family.

steps.body: Do one small thing this week to make a newer family member feel welcome.

lessons.title: Celebrate Your Family
lessons.summary: Notice and celebrate what’s good in your family.

steps.title: Families need good moments too
steps.body: Families often only gather for problems or obligations. Celebrating wins, birthdays and little milestones together creates warm memories that carry you through harder times.

steps.prompt: Your mum just finished her first 5k at 62. What’s a lovely way to mark it?

options.text: A quick “well done” text.
options.why: Kind, but this is a big moment that deserves more.

options.text: Rally the family for a celebration breakfast and a card everyone signs.
options.why: Making a fuss shows how proud you all are, and creates a memory.

options.text: Wait to see if she mentions it.
options.why: She might not, and the moment could slip past.

steps.prompt: Make a fuss.
steps.why: Saying you’re proud out loud makes family members feel truly seen.

steps.prompt: Which family member has a win you could celebrate soon?
Match each milestone with a way to celebrate.
steps.why: Celebrating together builds a store of good memories, and reminds everyone they belong.

steps.body: Celebrate one family member’s win this week, however small.
